full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** I agree with the first pass. The behaviour looks like a real emergent pattern, not an artifact, but it isn't new.

**What the system is.** Rule 1 is the Nowak–May spatial Prisoner's Dilemma: each cell plays its 8 neighbours plus itself and copies the best scorer. Rule 2 is the "conformity" update. Szolnoki and Perc first introduced it to evolutionary social dilemmas, defining it as choosing the most frequent strategy observed by the player, instead of being guided by maximizing their personal payoffs. Several papers combine the payoff-driven and conformity-driven update rules into one mixed rule. One example is Szolnoki & Chen, "Competition and partnership between conformity and payoff-based imitations in social dilemmas". There, each player probabilistically uses one rule or the other, which is close to your "majority rule with probability 0.1 per step".

**What the sub-programs show, and why it matches the literature:**
- **Rule 1 alone:** with T=1.5 and S=−0.5, type entropy falls to 0.05. Defection essentially takes over and the lattice freezes. This is the expected result when the temptation is this high.
- **Rule 2 alone:** you get majority-vote coarsening (correlation length 11, almost perfectly mixed types).
- **Full program:** cooperators and defectors persist together (entropy 0.82, so the minority type is roughly 25%). There are fewer, compact domains, a short correlation length, and cells keep flipping back and forth.

That is the main documented result. Conformity enhances network reciprocity on rings and square lattices because conformists can form an effective surface tension around cooperative clusters that prevent the invasion of defectors. Follow-up work describes competition swayed in favor of cooperators by network reciprocity, further enhanced by smooth(er) interfaces that emerge due to the coordination of conformists. A related model found that conformism generally fosters ordered cooperative phases and may also lead to bistable behaviors. The ongoing flipping fits the cluster turnover known from Nowak–May dynamics, kept going here by the tension between majority vote and payoff imitation.

**Possible twists I checked:** Your payoff point (S=−0.5), synchronous updating, and every cell sometimes conforming (rather than a fixed group of conformists) are differences in the rules. They don't produce a different kind of pattern. None of the four measured features (domain count, correlation length, reversals, entropy) shows anything beyond conformity rescuing cooperation in compact, fluctuating clusters.

**Is it an artifact?** No. The full program differs from both single-rule sub-programs, and the effects hold at 4× area and 3× run length. One caveat: the knock-out comparison is weak evidence. With every interaction rule removed, the lattice is just the frozen random starting pattern, which by construction has entropy of about 1, correlation length of about 1 and no reversals. The sub-program comparison is the one that matters, and it supports a real effect.

**Searches I ran:** "Szolnoki Perc conformity enhances network reciprocity prisoner's dilemma" and "Javarone conformity-driven agents support ordered phases spatial prisoner's dilemma". I only saw search-result snippets and did not open the full papers. The Szolnoki & Chen paper appeared only as a related-work listing, so I haven't checked its details.
